thread.title: 4 Myths About Alphabet To Squash Right Now - Alphabet, Inc. Cl A (NASDAQ:GOOGL)

author: Michael Henage
title: 4 Myths About Alphabet To Squash Right Now - Alphabet, Inc. Cl A (NASDAQ:GOOGL)

organizations.name: myths about alphabet to squash right now - alphabet, inc

text:
If you ask most investors to describe Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ), what you'll likely get is the company is growing, is drowning in cash, and has been a great investment. If you ask those same individuals why Alphabet doesn't pay a dividend when some of its peers do, they will likely point to the need for cash for acquisitions or internal growth. The truth is, Alphabet should already be paying a dividend, and there are four myths that investors need to squash right away.
Myth: Alphabet is a better investment because it reinvests money back into the company instead of paying a dividend Growth investors will normally say they don't care if a company pays a dividend. The theory is, a fast-growing company should reinvest its earnings to fuel future growth. On the surface, it seems that Alphabet is doing exactly that, as the company's most recent quarter showed an adjusted EPS gain of more than 28%.
According to Yahoo Finance, analysts expect Alphabet to generate average annual EPS growth over the next five years nearly 17%. By comparison, its large-cap peers like Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) and Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT ) are expected to grow annual EPS during that same time frame by 13% and 12% respectively. If Alphabet is reinvesting cash for future growth instead of paying a dividend, the stock must have outperformed its dividend paying peers, right?
The somewhat surprising answer has been no. Investors in Alphabet have been treated to a better than 21% five-year compound annual growth rate (CAGR) on their investment. While this is an excellent result, Apple's five-year CAGR sits north of 23%, and Microsoft beat both companies, producing an over 26% return.
What's even more telling is a comparison of Alphabet vs. Microsoft during 2018. We can clearly see that Microsoft's stock is less volatile. It's a well-known fact that when the market declines, companies with dividends usually hold up better because as the stock price declines, the yield increases. Looking at the chart, Alphabet's investors are being led on a bumpy ride to a lesser return.
(Source Yahoo Finance)
Myth: Alphabet's valuation doesn't matter because it's growing faster Like an ostrich with its head stuck in the sand, some investors buy growth stocks without paying attention to valuation. While it is traditionally true that investors may need to pay a premium for high-quality growth, no stock is immune to valuation concerns forever.
Using the PEG+Y ratio allows us to consider each company's earnings growth and yield and compare this combined return with the forward P/E ratio. Let's see how Alphabet stacks up to its peers. Keep in mind, the higher the PEG+Y, the better relative value investors should be getting.

In short, Alphabet appears to be a lesser value than Apple, yet analysts have been lowering estimates for the company's earnings. Where Microsoft is concerned, it seems the stock may have gotten ahead of itself, yet estimates have been going up.
The bottom line here is, investors seem to already be paying a premium for Alphabet shares. Yet, the 30+ analysts that follow the company are less enthusiastic about next year's earnings growth. Instituting a dividend would improve Alphabet's relative value immediately.
Myth: Alphabet prefers to do acquisitions with cash; paying a dividend might cause the company to go into debt for purchases, hurting its cash flow At present, Alphabet is generating significant free cash flow above its expenses (more on that in a moment) and sits on $98.9 billion in cash net of long-term debt. Some rumored acquisition targets that would require the use of this cash are Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX ) and Twitter (NYSE: TWTR ). Both targets provide equally ridiculous arguments for the use of cash.
Netflix's current market cap sits north of $180 billion, even if Alphabet used all of its cash, it would either have to finance the rest with debt or issue stock. On the other end of the spectrum, Twitter's current market cap is around $35 billion. Even if Alphabet paid a premium and bid $50 billion, the company would still have $49 billion left over.
Just to eliminate this myth even further. If we look at historical acquisitions by Alphabet and add up the 10 largest, it becomes clear the company's cash on hand is more than sufficient. Some of these acquisitions are key cogs in the Google machine such as: YouTube, DoubleClick, and Waze. On the other hand, some are questionable uses of cash such as Motorola Mobility and Nest Labs. No matter what you believe about each acquisition, the top 10 deals over the last 10+ years cost a total of $25.2 billion. To put this in perspective, Alphabet could do these deals almost four times over and just barely use up all of its current cash on hand.
In case investors think that Alphabet is sitting on an unusually large amount of cash, the company sits in between its peers when it comes to cash value per share. At last count, Alphabet's cash per share works out to about 12%. Apple has net cash per share of 18% of the current price, while Microsoft's cash represents roughly 7.4% .
It seems clear that Alphabet has enough cash to do even a very large transaction like Twitter. The theory that the company would issue debt makes little sense, as Alphabet's market cap is over $800 billion. The company's best currency besides cash would be its shares.
Myth: Alphabet's cash flow isn't sufficient to pay a dividend and grow the company While it's true that Alphabet's free cash flow took at hit in the current quarter, that was primarily due to the company's massive increase in capital expenditures (capex) versus last year. Capex jumped 192% year-over-year, yet even with this massive increase, the company still generated roughly $1.4 billion in core free cash flow. Under a more normalized capex situation, the company would have generated as much as $6 billion in core free cash flow.
Looking again at our comparatives, Alphabet produced normalized core free cash flow roughly $0.20 per $1 of revenue. Using this same measure, Apple generated $0.22 per $1 of revenue, and Microsoft produced $0.27.
Just to put this myth to bed, Alphabet's core free cash flow has been significant for a while. If we look at just the last three years, in 2017, the company produced over $6 billion in core free cash flow. In 2016, free cash flow exceeded $15 billion, and in 2015, the company generated over $11 billion. During this same time frame, Alphabet has spent an increasing amount buying back shares.
The short version is, Alphabet is generating significant free cash flow and has been for years. Attempting to say the company can't afford a dividend seems to be more of a myth than a reality.
How much? The key question would be how much could Alphabet afford to pay without affecting its cash flow? Apple uses just 20% of its core free cash flow to cover its dividend, and Microsoft uses about 44%. Alphabet already uses funds to repurchase shares; what if those funds went toward a dividend instead?
In the current quarter, Alphabet used about 35% of its core free cash flow on share repurchases. If this $2.2 billion were turned into a dividend, shareholders would receive around $3 per quarter or $12 per year. This would give the stock a current yield of about 1%. While that doesn't sound like a lot, this would open the stock up to mutual funds and individuals who only buy shares of companies with dividends. This would also potentially create a floor for the stock when the market corrects as the yield would increase as the price declines. Last, given Alphabet's strong cash flow, the dividend could be increased steadily, thus generating more demand for the shares.
Though Alphabet is known for acquisitions, it makes sense a steady dividend commitment might cause the company to look more carefully at some acquisition targets (Motorola Mobility anyone?). Alphabet's refusal to consider a dividend reminds me of a favorite re-quote that Peter Lynch used in his book One Up On Wall Street , quoting Hugh Liedtke of Pennzoil: "the more cash that builds up in the treasury, the greater the pressure to piss it away."
Disclosure: I am/we are long MSFT, AAPL.
